items.text: In this lesson you go to a networking event and talk to people you have never met. You learn how to start a conversation, keep it going and steer it where you want it to go, with small words like actually, mind you and granted. Then you read an article about small talk at work and write a follow-up message to someone you met.

Welcome to Level 4. In this first lesson, you are at a networking event. It's a room full of people who work in the same area, or who want to meet people who do. Most of them don't know each other. For many people, the hardest part is the first sentence. So start with an easy question. So, how do you know the organiser? What brings you here tonight? Then listen for something you have in common: the same line of work, the same town, or a friend you both know. Listen to Priya and Tomasz. They have never met before. Notice how they keep the conversation going, and how they move it from one topic to the next.

The grammar in this lesson is about small words that do a big job. Actually corrects something gently, or adds a surprise. I'm not in sales, actually. I'm in logistics. Mind you adds a but to what you have just said, without taking it back. The venue's lovely. Mind you, it's a bit noisy. Granted agrees with part of a point before you argue on. Granted, it's a long way. But it's worth it. Anyway moves the conversation on, or brings it back to the main topic. Anyway, what do you do? The second point is tags. You work with Kwame, don't you? A tag checks something you think is true. If your voice goes down, you are fairly sure. If it goes up, you really want to know. An echo question shows interest. I've just moved here from Leeds. Have you? What made you move?

In Section 3, you read an article about small talk at work. Some people think it's a waste of time. The writer disagrees. She explains how a two-minute chat by the kettle helps colleagues trust each other, especially when a team works from home. Read it once, quickly, for the main idea. Then read it again for the details: who says what, and what they suggest. Then you write a short follow-up message to someone you met. Say where you met, mention something you talked about, and suggest a next step. Keep it friendly, and keep it short.

Then it's your turn. In the live class, you meet three people. Start each conversation, find one thing you have in common, and arrange to follow up. Don't worry about perfect grammar. Ask questions, listen to the answers, and use them in your next question. Use the other person's name once or twice. It helps you remember it, and most people like hearing their own name. If there's a silence, change the subject. What do you do when you're not working? At the end, swap details and say what happens next. I'll drop you a line next week.

Last, you read a longer text linked to this lesson. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions. Notice how the people in it start a conversation, and how they keep it going.

Anyway, I mustn't keep you.
It's been really good to meet you.

Words that steer: actually, mind you, granted, anyway. Actually corrects gently, or adds a surprise: I'm not in sales, actually. I'm in logistics. Mind you adds a but and keeps your first point standing: It's a great venue. Mind you, it's a bit loud. Granted agrees with part of a point before you argue on: Granted, it's expensive. But it saves time. Anyway moves the talk on, or back to the main topic: Anyway, what brings you here? They belong to speech and friendly messages. In a formal report, use however or in fact.

In this lesson you explain a new product to a colleague who has never seen it, and you learn to say exactly what you mean. You see how prefixes and suffixes build new words, so you can work out words you have never met. Then you read a job specification full of jargon and rewrite it in plain English.

In this lesson, you explain something new to someone who has never seen it. Listen to Ana and Samir. They work at a busy car repair garage. The garage has bought a new booking app, and Ana explains it to Samir. Samir is great with engines, but he isn't very technical with computers. So Ana has to be clear. Listen for three useful phrases. It's a kind of… gives the general idea first, by comparing the new thing with something familiar. It's a kind of online diary. Basically… gives the main point in a few words. Basically, customers book their own appointments. What I mean is… says it again, more precisely, when your first try was vague. What I mean is, if you can send a text, you can use it. A good explanation moves from the general to the precise, and it checks that the listener is following.

The grammar in this lesson is about building words. Many long English words are short words with extra parts. A part at the start is a prefix. Un- and dis- often mean not. Able, unable. Agree, disagree. Mis- means wrongly. Read, misread. A part at the end is a suffix. -able means you can do it: readable, affordable. -ful means full of something: useful, helpful. -ness turns an adjective into a noun: kind, kindness. So when you meet a long word you don't know, split it into parts. Unreadable: un, read, able. It cannot be read. Carelessness: care, less, ness. Not taking care. The second point is the small word that comes after some nouns and verbs. We say a reason for, a solution to, and depend on. It depends on the weather, not of the weather. Learn these pairs as one piece.

In Section 3, you read a job specification. It describes a job, and it lists what the employer wants from applicants. Like many job specifications, it is full of jargon: words that only people in that line of work understand. Escalate. Triage. First-line resolution. Your task is to rewrite it in plain English. Use short sentences and everyday words. Keep every fact, but say it so that anyone can follow it. Here is a good test. Could a friend outside that job read your version once and understand it?

Then it's your turn. Choose a topic you know well: a tool from your job, a process, or a hobby. Explain it to someone who knows nothing about it. Start with the general idea. Give one clear example. Then say it more precisely. Your listener will ask questions. Listen carefully to each one. If your first answer was vague, try again: What I mean is… And check as you go. Does that make sense so far?

Last, you read a longer text linked to this lesson. As you read, stop at one or two long words. Split them into parts, and work out what they mean before you check. You'll be surprised how often it works.

That depends on how old their phone is.
In practice, they just phone us instead.
I'll demonstrate it on Friday.

Building words: un-, dis-, mis-, -able, -ful, -ness. un- and dis- mean not, or the opposite: unable, unfair, dishonest, disagree, disconnect. mis- means wrongly: misread, misunderstand, misspell, mislead. -able means you can do it: readable, affordable, washable. Add un- for the opposite: unreadable. -ful means full of it: useful, helpful, stressful. Its opposite, -less, means without it: useless, careless. -ness makes a noun from an adjective: kind, kindness. Aware, awareness. Careless, carelessness.

items.text: A reason for, depend on: the small word that belongs. Some nouns always bring the same small word: a reason for, a solution to, an increase in, an effect on. Some verbs do too: depend on, apply for, deal with, rely on, listen to. Learn the pair as one piece: the reason for the delay, not the reason of the delay. Some verbs take no small word at all: discuss the plan, not discuss about the plan. After the small word, use -ing for an action: the reason for changing.

Everyone's talking about this new app. What is it, exactly?
It's a kind of online diary. Basically, customers book their own appointments on their phones.
OK. But what's the reason for changing? The paper diary works, doesn't it?
Not always. Half the time the handwriting's unreadable, and people misread the times. Last month we had nine double bookings.
Nine? I had no idea. So whose fault was that?
Nobody's, really. It wasn't carelessness. The paper system just isn't reliable.
And is the app hard to use? I'm good with engines, but I'm not very technical with computers.
Not at all. It's really user-friendly. What I mean is, if you can send a text, you can use it.
Will customers need a new phone for it?
That depends on how old their phone is. It's compatible with almost any smartphone. And it sends a reminder the day before, which is really useful.
That sounds handy. What happens if the internet goes down?
Then customers are unable to book online until it's back. In practice, they just phone us instead.
Fair enough. When does it start?
We launch it on Monday. I'll demonstrate it to everyone on Friday afternoon.
So what do you actually do all day? Your job title means nothing to me!
I'm a quantity surveyor. Basically, I look after the money on building projects.
What, like an accountant?
It's a kind of accountant, but for buildings. I work out what a building will cost before anyone starts.
How can you know that before it's built?
Let me give you an example. For a new block of flats, I count everything on the drawings: every brick, every window, every hour of work.
Every brick? That sounds endless.
It would be, but the software does most of the counting. What I mean is, I check the numbers and the prices, and I make sure nothing is missing.
And what happens if the costs go up halfway through?
That depends on the contract. Usually, I agree any changes with the client before the builders carry on.
So you're the person who says no to expensive ideas?
Sometimes! But mostly I help people find a cheaper way to get what they want. Does that make sense?
Completely. I finally understand your job!

In this lesson you tell a story over dinner and make your friends want to hear the end. You use the four perfect forms to make the order of events clear, and verbs like claimed, admitted, urged and denied to report what people said. Then you read a witness statement and meeting minutes, and write one event from two points of view.

In this lesson, you tell a story. Not a report, but the kind of story you tell friends over dinner. Listen to Mei. She tells her friend Omar about a strange morning at work. Notice how she starts: You'll never believe what happened to me on Friday. That makes Omar want to hear the rest. Then listen for two useful phrases. It turned out that… gives the surprise, the thing that was really true. It turned out that he'd been waiting at the other station. Apparently… tells people you heard this from someone else, so you can't be completely sure. Apparently, my manager had put the wrong station in the email. Good storytellers also leave out the boring parts. To cut a long story short, we were twenty minutes late.

The grammar in this lesson has two parts. The first is the four perfect forms. Two of them reach up to now. I've waited an hour: that's the fact. I've been waiting an hour: that's the activity, and how long it has gone on. The other two reach up to a moment in the past. The meeting had started when I arrived. I'd been waiting for forty minutes when he rang. So ask yourself two questions. Does it reach up to now, or up to a moment in the past? And do you mean the finished fact, or the activity going on? The second part is reporting verbs. Said is neutral. Claimed suggests you're not sure it's true. Admitted means someone accepted something they didn't want to say. Urged means advised strongly. Denied means said it wasn't true. Choose carefully. The verb you choose shows what you think.

In Section 3, you read two documents about the same event at a warehouse: a witness statement, and the minutes of a meeting. Read them side by side. Where do they agree? Where do they contradict each other? And is every verb fair, or does one of them take sides? Look closely at the reporting verbs. Stated is neutral. Claimed is not, so ask yourself whether the writer had a reason to doubt. Then you write about one event from two points of view. Tell it first as one person saw it, then as the other person saw it. Keep the order of events clear, and choose your reporting verbs carefully.

Then it's your turn. Think of a story someone told you: a friend, a colleague or a neighbour. Choose one with two or more people who didn't agree. Retell it in the live class. Report what each person said, and also what they meant. Be fair to both sides. If you're not sure something is true, say so: apparently, or she claimed. Your listeners will ask you questions, so make sure you know the order of events.
Last, you read a longer story linked to this lesson. As you read, ask yourself who is telling it. Is the storyteller fair to everyone? Would another person in the story tell it differently?

The four perfect forms. Up to now, the fact: I've waited an hour. He's told the story five times. Up to now, the activity: I've been waiting an hour. He's been telling everyone. Up to a moment in the past, the fact: When I arrived, the meeting had started. Up to a moment in the past, the activity: I'd been waiting for forty minutes when he rang. A number of finished things takes the simple form: I've sent three emails, not I've been sending three emails.

You'll never believe what happened to me on Friday.
Go on, tell me.
My manager asked me to meet a new client at the station. A Mr Adeyemi, coming from Birmingham for a big meeting.
That sounds simple enough.
That's what I thought. I'd been waiting on the platform for forty minutes, and there was no sign of him.
Had his train been cancelled?
No! It turned out that he'd been waiting at the other station, on the far side of town. Apparently, my manager had put the wrong station in the email.
What a mix-up! So how did you find him?
Well, believe it or not, I went into a café to ring him, and he was sitting at the next table. He'd taken a taxi to come and find me!
That's bizarre. What a coincidence!
To cut a long story short, we were twenty minutes late for the meeting. At first my manager denied it was her fault. She claimed the email was perfectly clear.
And was it?
Not at all. She's since admitted her mistake. Luckily, Mr Adeyemi thought it was hilarious. He's been telling everyone the story ever since.
You'll never believe what my neighbour told me yesterday.
Go on.
Samir had been waiting all week for a new laptop. The tracking said it had been delivered, but there was nothing at his door.
Oh no. Had someone stolen it?
That's what he thought. Apparently, he went straight to the woman next door, Ana, and asked if she'd taken it in.
And had she?
She denied it. She said she'd been at work all day. But Samir said another neighbour had seen her with a big box.
So who was right?
Well, it turned out that the box was hers. She'd ordered a new chair. Samir's laptop had been left at the wrong address, three streets away.
What a mix-up! Did he apologise?
He did. And to be fair to him, he wasn't accusing her. What he meant was, he hoped she had it, so it was safe.
So they're still friends?
Better than ever. They've been laughing about it all week, and he's offered to help her build the chair.

Everyone has made a decision they still think about: a job they took or turned down, a move, a risk. In this lesson you look back on decisions like these, say what might have happened if you had chosen differently, and talk about regrets without sounding stuck in the past. You also read a column about a big life decision and write a reflective paragraph of your own.

This lesson is about decisions, and about looking back on them. First, you listen to Priya and her colleague Tomasz. Two years ago, Priya had a dilemma. She could stay in a safe job, or move to a new city for a job she really wanted. Listen to how she talks about it now. She says: If I'd known how lonely the first winter would be, I might have waited a year. She says: I wish I'd asked more questions. And she says: I needn't have sold my car. Notice that she is not complaining. She is thinking out loud. That is a very natural thing to do in English, with friends and at work.

Next, the grammar. There are two parts. Part one is the third conditional. It is about the past, and about something that did not happen. If I had known, I would have waited. I did not know, so I did not wait. A mixed conditional joins a past choice to the present. If I hadn't moved, I wouldn't be here now. Part two is regret. Say: I wish I had asked. Or, stronger: If only I had asked. Never say: I wish I would have asked. Last, a small pair. I needn't have worried means I worried, and it was not necessary. I didn't need to worry means it was not necessary, and usually I didn't.

Then you read a column from a magazine. A columnist writes about their own life, in their own voice. This writer left a stable job to start again in another city. She tells you what she gave up, what went wrong, and what she learned. Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again for the details. After that, you write a reflective paragraph about a decision of your own. Say what you decided, what you gave up, and how you see it now. Use one conditional and one wish.

In the live class, you talk through a real decision. It can be big or small: a job, a move, a course, a car, even a haircut. Say what you did and why. Say what might have happened if you had chosen differently. Then say what you learned. Your teacher and the other learners will ask you questions, so be ready to explain your reasons. Try to sound calm and thoughtful. Looking back is not about blame. It is about understanding.

Last, you read a longer text about a turning point in someone's life. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions. Watch for the sentences that look back: if only, I wish, if she had known. Writers often use them at the moments that matter most. Ask yourself: at which moment could things have gone differently? Every day, news reaches us from newspapers, websites, friends and social media, and not all of it is true. In this lesson you discuss a news story, learn how reports and headlines say who is claiming what, and compare one story told by three different outlets. At the end, you present a story yourself and say how far you trust it, and why.

This lesson is about the news, and about how far to trust it. First, you listen to two colleagues, Mei and Carlos. A story about their town has gone viral on social media, and Carlos is worried. Listen to how they talk about it. They do not just repeat the story. They say where it came from. According to the local paper… Apparently… I read somewhere that… These phrases are important. They tell the listener how close you are to the facts. Notice that Mei is sceptical. She wants to know the source before she believes anything, and she does not share the story until she knows more.

Next, the grammar. There are two parts. Part one is the reporting passive. News reports use it all the time. It is said that the factory will close. The director is thought to be leaving. These sentences report a claim, but they do not say whose claim it is. So always ask: said by whom? Part two is how headlines work. Headlines use very few words, and they have their own grammar. Factory closes means the factory has closed, or is closing. Jobs cut means jobs have been cut. Minister to resign means the minister is going to resign. Read a headline carefully, and then read the story under it.

Then you read one story, reported by three different outlets: a local newspaper, a news website and a popular gossip site. The facts are the same, but the stories are not. Look at the headlines. Look at who each report quotes. A named spokesperson? An anonymous source? Nobody at all? Then look at what each outlet has checked. One says clearly what it could not verify. Another calls its story exclusive, but gives you very little to check. After that, you write a short report of your own. Say who claims what, and what has not been checked yet.

In the live class, you present a news story. It can be from your country, your town or your work. Choose a story you know well. First, tell the story briefly. Then say where it came from and how much you trust it. Give your reasons. Is the source named? Have other outlets checked it? Does anybody gain from the story? The other learners will ask you questions, so be ready. You do not need to be sure. It is fine to say: I'd take it with a pinch of salt.

Last, you read a longer text connected with the news. It may be a story, an article or a chapter of a book. Read it once for the main story. Then read it again and answer the questions. As you read, ask the questions from this lesson: who is speaking, how do they know, and what might they not be saying?

Charts and figures are everywhere at work, from team meetings to reports and the news. In this lesson you learn to describe numbers and trends accurately, to talk about what will happen next, and to say clearly what a set of figures does and does not show. At the end, you present a chart from your own work or life and answer questions about it.

This lesson is about numbers, and how to talk about them clearly. First, you listen to a team update. Samir leads a customer service team, and he is showing his colleague Lena some charts. Listen to how he describes the lines on the chart. Calls rose steadily. They reached a peak in May. Then they levelled off. Listen, too, for the small words that say how exact a figure is: about, roughly, just over half, nearly twenty. Notice that Lena asks good questions. What was it last year? Is there anything that worries you? You will ask questions like these in the live class.

Next, the grammar. There are two parts. Part one is describing change. Two small words matter a lot here. By gives the size of the change. To gives the new number. Sales rose by ten per cent. Sales rose to five hundred. You can also make a noun: a rise of ten per cent. Part two is looking ahead. This time next year, we will be using the new system. That means it will already be happening then. By 2030, the number will have doubled. That means it will be finished before then. Listen for these forms in the conversation, and then practise them.

Then you read a short report. A company asked its staff how they travel to work, and the report gives the results. Read it for the main idea first. Then read it again slowly. The numbers are important. Pay special attention to the part called Limitations. Good reports say what their figures cannot show: who did not answer, what was left out, and what is only an estimate. The numbers in a report are only as good as the way they were collected. After that, you write a summary of the report. Give the main figures, and then say clearly what its limits are.

In the live class, you present a chart from your work or your life. It could be sales, customers, your electricity bills, your running times, or the hours you study English. You have two minutes. Say what the chart shows, describe the main trend, and point out one interesting detail. Then say one thing the chart does not show. After that, the others ask you questions. Try to answer with exact figures. Prepare carefully. Check every number before the class, and practise saying the big ones out loud: four hundred and fifty, just over three thousand, seventy-five per cent.

Last, you read a longer text connected with facts and figures. Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again and answer the questions. When you meet a number, ask yourself: where does it come from, and what does it really show? Numbers can be exact and still tell only part of the story.

In this lesson, you talk about why things happen and what they lead to, without claiming more than you know. You listen to two council workers discussing a local problem, read an article about a reservoir that is running dry, and write a balanced paragraph. Then you discuss a problem in your own area and agree on the likeliest cause.

In this lesson, we talk about causes and effects: why something happens, and what it leads to. We start in a council office. Lena and Omar work for the council. Complaints about a local park have doubled, and they want to know why. Listen to how carefully they speak. Omar says: It could be that this is the root cause. He does not say: This caused it. He isn't sure yet, so he doesn't claim it. Listen for three phrases. It could be that. This is likely to. And which in turn. Which in turn joins a chain of effects. Litter attracts rats, which in turn puts people off using the park. You also learn words for causes. A factor is one cause among several. The root cause is the deepest one, the cause behind the others.

The grammar has two parts. The first is hedging. Hedging means showing how sure you are. May, might and could mean: it's possible. The new flats may be a factor. Tends to means: this usually happens. Litter tends to attract rats. Is likely to means: this will probably happen. The problem is likely to get worse. The second part is cause and effect. Lead to and result in join a cause to its effect. The cuts led to fewer collections. Fewer collections resulted in more litter. Which in turn adds the next step in the chain. One small point: after may and might, the verb never takes an s. Say: It may cause problems. Not: It may causes problems.

Next, you read a news article about a reservoir that is running dry. Many people want one simple answer. The article gives three: the weather, the amount of water we use, and leaking pipes. Notice how it deals with climate change. Long, dry summers are likely to become more common. But no single summer can be blamed on climate change alone. That is a balanced view. It gives each cause its place, and it doesn't claim more than the facts show. The article also builds a chain with words for the environment. A new plant would need a lot of energy. Unless that energy is renewable, emissions go up, which in turn adds to climate change. Then you write a balanced paragraph of your own, about an environmental problem you know. Give more than one cause, say how sure you are, and finish carefully.

In the task, you discuss a local problem in a group. It could be late buses, noise at night, or rents going up. Each person may have a different idea about the cause. That's normal, and it's useful. Ask for evidence, and be fair to other ideas. You can say: That's probably part of it, but… Or: To some extent, yes. Here is an example. One person says: I think one factor might be the roadworks. Another answers: That's probably part of it, but the buses are late on Sundays too. That is evidence, and it helps the group decide. Then agree on two things: the likeliest cause, and one action you can take or ask for. One clear action is better than five vague ones.

Last, you read a longer text about causes and effects in health, the environment or society. As you read, keep asking one question: does the writer prove this, or only suggest it? Look for the careful words: may, might, likely, partly. A writer who uses them is often more honest, not less. Then talk or write about it. Which claims did you believe, and why?

In this lesson, you learn to write so that your reader can follow you without any effort. You listen to a colleague giving feedback on a draft email, compare two versions of a complaint letter, and write a four-paragraph opinion essay. Then you edit a real text of your own and explain your changes.

This lesson is about writing that flows: writing that your reader can follow without any effort. We start with feedback. Tomasz has written an email to the whole office about a move to a new building. Before he sends it, his colleague Amina reads the draft. She is honest, but kind. First, she says what is good: the information is all there, and the tone is friendly. Then she names the problem: it's hard to follow. Listen for two phrases. It jumps from the parking to the new desks. And: How about starting with the date of the move? Notice that every criticism comes with a suggestion. That is what makes feedback constructive. You also learn words for talking about writing: the structure, the wording, and the topic sentence that opens each paragraph.

The grammar has two parts. The first is linking words. Although and whereas join two ideas inside one sentence. Although it's interesting, it doesn't help. The old office had parking, whereas the new one doesn't. However and therefore are different. They start a new sentence, and they have a comma after them. The lifts will be closed. However, the stairs will be open. So never join two full sentences with just a comma and however. That is the mistake Amina spotted. The second part is pointing back. In the phrase this means that, the word this points back to a whole idea. And such a big change points back to something you have just described. These small words are what hold a paragraph together.

Next, you read two letters about the same problem: repairs to a rented flat. The first letter is angry and hard to follow. It jumps from the window to the light, and back to the window. It never says what the writer wants. The second letter says what he wants at the start: a date for each repair. Then it takes the problems one by one. It even accepts that one visit failed because he was out. Notice the small words in the second letter: Firstly, Secondly, However, Therefore. They show the reader the shape of the letter from the start. Which letter would you answer first? Then you write an opinion essay in four paragraphs: your opinion, your main reason with an example, the other side, and your conclusion.

In the task, you work on a real text of your own. It could be an email, a report, or the essay you have just written. Edit it so it flows. Put the ideas in a clear order. Start each paragraph with a topic sentence. Link the ideas, and check the punctuation. Then explain three changes to a partner. Say what you changed, and why. For example: In my first version, it jumped from the kitchen to the car park. Or: I cut out this sentence, because it didn't help the reader. Your partner may ask: Why did you move that paragraph? Answer with a reason: Because the reader needs the date first.

Last, you read a longer text. This time, read it as a writer as well as a reader. How does the writer move from one idea to the next? Which words link the paragraphs? Good writers use the same tools you practised in this lesson: a clear order, linking words, and words that point back. Find one part that flows well, and one part you would tighten up. Then talk or write about it.

In this lesson, you learn to argue for what you believe and to answer the other side fairly. You listen to a team debating whether to keep flexitime, read a group's response to a plan to close a library, and write your own response to a proposal. Then you take part in a structured debate in the live class.

This lesson is about making a case: arguing for what you believe, and answering the other side fairly. We start at a team meeting. The team has tried flexitime for three months, and now they must decide whether to keep it. Carlos is for it. Mei has an objection. Priya, the manager, has to decide. Listen to how they disagree without getting angry. Carlos says: The main reason is that people are happier. Mei answers: That may be true, but three months isn't very long. Then listen for the moment when Mei says: OK, I'll concede that. She accepts one point, and moves on to a stronger one. You also learn words for a debate. A drawback is a disadvantage. If the benefits outweigh a drawback, they matter more. And to back something up is to give evidence for it.

The grammar has two parts. The first is the shape of a good argument. A claim says what you think: we should keep flexitime. A reason says why: the main reason is that people get more done. Evidence is a fact that others can check: sick days fell by a third. Be careful here. Say: the main reason is that. Don't say: the main reason is because. The second part is conceding. Admittedly accepts a point for the other side. Admittedly, the trial was short. Even so gives your view again. Even so, the results were clear. On the other hand gives a different side. Conceding one real point makes the rest of your case stronger, not weaker.

Next, you read a response to a consultation. The council wants to close a small library, and it has asked local people for their views. A group of residents writes back. Notice how they do it. First, they accept what is true: the council must save money. Then they say where they disagree. Then they give evidence: numbers, not just feelings. And they finish with a proposal, not a threat. Words like acknowledge, reconsider and in principle help you to sound firm, but polite. Then you write your own response to a proposal. It can be a real one from your area or your work, or you can invent it.

The task is a real debate in the live class. The topic is working from home two days a week. You are in a team, for or against. First, give your case: a claim, a reason and evidence. Then the other team answers, and here is the key skill. Don't just repeat yourself. Concede one point, clearly, and then counter it. For example: That may be true, and I'll concede that new staff need support. Even so, the evidence suggests that the team works well. Don't concede something small that nobody cares about. Concede the other side's best point, and then show why your case is still stronger. At the end, the class votes.

Last, you read a longer text in which someone makes a case. As you read, look for the claim, the reasons and the evidence. Does the writer answer the other side, or ignore it? Is the evidence something you could check, or only a feeling? Then talk or write about it. Who do you agree with, and why?

In this lesson you negotiate a delivery with a supplier, set conditions and look for a compromise that both sides can accept. You also read a set of terms and conditions, write an email proposing a fair solution, and then negotiate a real deal: a price, a date and a condition.

In this lesson, you negotiate. You set conditions, and you reach an agreement that both sides can accept. First, you listen to Priya. She buys supplies for a small chain of cafés, and they're opening a new branch. She's on a call with Tomasz, from their coffee supplier. Priya wants a lower price. Tomasz wants a bigger order. Neither of them gets everything, and that's the point. A good negotiation ends in a compromise. Listen for the phrases that move things forward. What if we ordered two hundred kilos? Would you consider twelve pounds a kilo? In return, we could sign for six months. Notice that nobody simply says no. They say: yes, provided that…

Now the grammar. There are two points. First, the words that set a condition. Provided that, and as long as, mean only if. We'll deliver on the twenty-eighth, provided that you confirm by Friday. Unless means if not. Unless you confirm by Friday, I can't promise the date. Don't add another not. Unless already has one inside it. Supposing, and what if, put an idea on the table. Supposing we split the difference? Here's the trap. After provided, as long as and unless, use the present, even when you mean the future. As long as you confirm. Not: as long as you will confirm. Second: the more, the better. The more you order, the lower the price. Both halves start with the, and then a comparative.

Next, you read a supplier's terms and conditions. Terms are written in numbered clauses. Don't read them like a story. Use them like a map, and find the clause you need. Ask three questions. What must I do? What am I entitled to? And what happens if something goes wrong: a penalty, a discount, or a replacement at no extra cost? Look out for provided, unless and as long as. That's usually where the real condition is. Then you write an email that proposes a compromise. Say what happened, name the clause, suggest a solution, and offer something in return.

Then it's your turn to negotiate, in the live class or with Wehel. Your company needs three hundred T-shirts for a charity race. The price is too high, and the delivery date is too late. You must agree a price, a date and one condition. Prepare before you start. Know your ideal price, and your limit. Decide what you can offer in return: a deposit, or collecting the shirts yourself. Stay polite, and stay firm. If they won't budge on the price, change the question. Talk about the date, or the payment, instead. And at the end, sum up the deal. So, just to check…

Last, you read a longer story or article about a negotiation. Read it once for the main events. Then read it again, and notice what each side wanted, and what each side gave up. Ask yourself: was the final deal fair? Would you have done anything differently?

In this lesson you make a formal phone call, and then you put what you want in writing. You learn how to make your English more formal without making it hard to read, and you read a formal letter and a short report. At the end, you write a report that recommends one of two options, and you present it.

In this lesson, you write formally: letters, emails and short reports. But first, a phone call. Amina manages the office of a small design studio. The company van needs a parking permit, and the council has refused it. She calls to find out why. Listen to how she starts. I'm calling on behalf of Brightside Design, regarding our application. Regarding is a formal way to say about. The officer can't change the decision on the phone. So Amina says: I'll put it in writing. A letter gives both sides a record of what was asked, and when. Notice the useful phone phrases too. Could you put me through? Please hold the line. Could you give me a reference for this call?

Now the grammar. Formality isn't one switch. It works more like a set of dials. Dial one: full forms. Not we haven't, but we have not. Dial two: formal words. Not ask, but enquire. Not tell, but notify. Dial three: the passive. Not we've received your form, but your form has been received. Notices use the passive all the time. Visitors are asked to sign in. This door must be kept closed. But don't turn every dial up. Very long sentences and old-fashioned words make a letter hard to read. Then, formal links. In which case means if that happens. You may appeal, in which case the decision will be reviewed. Whereby means by which. The council has a scheme whereby businesses can pay monthly.

Next, you read two documents: the council's reply to Amina, and a short report that she wrote for her director. Look at the layout. The letter has a heading, so you know at once what it's about. The report has numbered sections, and bullet points for each option. Then you write your own formal letter. Remember the pairs. Dear Sir or Madam goes with Yours faithfully. Dear Ms Yusuf goes with Yours sincerely. Finally, test your letter on a reader. Can they say, in one sentence, what you want? If they can't, rewrite it.

Then you write and present a short report. You compare two options, and you recommend one. It could be two suppliers, two venues for a staff event, or two phone contracts. Keep the shape simple: the purpose, option A, option B, and your recommendation. For each option, give the cost, one advantage and one disadvantage. Then choose. A report that recommends nothing doesn't help anybody. When you present it, speak more simply than you write. Say we and you. Finish with one clear next step, and a date. Then take questions. If you don't know an answer, say so, and offer to find out.

Last, you read a longer story or article linked to formal writing. Read it once for the main events. Then read it again, and notice who writes to whom, and whether the writing works for its reader. Look at the choices each writer makes: the greeting, the layout and the words.

At which point = and at that moment: No reply was received by 14 May, at which point the file was closed. Whereby = by which, through which: The council has a scheme whereby businesses pay monthly. Put a comma before in which case and at which point. Whereby follows a noun: a scheme, a system, an agreement. They belong in letters and reports. In a friendly email, they sound stiff.

This is the last lesson of the Intensive English course. You give a short talk, handle questions and lead a discussion, and you write a plan for your English for the next six months. At the end, you give a five-minute presentation and take the B2 check.

This is the last lesson of the course. In it, you give a talk, you lead a discussion, and you plan your English for after the course. First, you listen to Mei. She leads a customer service team, and her team has just finished a trial of a live chat service. She presents the results at a team meeting. Listen to how she guides her audience. I'd like to start by giving you an overview. Moving on to the feedback. To sum up. These phrases are signposts. They tell the listener where they are in the talk. Then listen to how she answers questions. That's a good question. Off the top of my head, I'd say four, but let me check.

Now the grammar. There are two points. First, signposts. You open: I'd like to start by. You move on: Moving on to. You point at a visual aid: As you can see on the chart. And you close: To sum up. Second, putting weight on an idea. In writing, you can use bold type. In speech, you use grammar. What matters is the result. The key idea comes at the end, after is. It was the team that made it work. The key idea comes straight after it was, and your voice stresses it. Don't use these in every sentence. Save them for the one or two ideas that you want people to remember.

Next, you read Ana's learning plan for the next six months. Notice three things. She chooses one priority, not five. She names a time and a place, not just an amount: a podcast on the train, not an hour a day. And she says what might go wrong. Then you write your own plan. Be honest about where you are, and make it realistic. A small plan that you follow is worth more than a big plan that you give up. Then check your plan with three questions. Is there only one priority? Does it name a time and a place? Would I still do it in a busy week?

Then you give a five-minute presentation, and you lead the discussion after it. Choose a topic you know well: a project at work, a change you'd like to see, or your plan for your English. Rehearse it out loud, twice, with a timer. Nerves are normal, and a slow first sentence helps. After the talk, you lead the discussion. Take questions. Ask the group a question of your own. And make sure everybody gets a turn. Then you take the B2 check, in listening, reading, writing and speaking. Take your time, and show what you can do.

Last, you read a longer story or article about speaking in front of others. Read it once for the main events. Then read it again, and notice how the speaker prepares, and how they deal with the unexpected. And then, well done. You've reached the end of the course. Keep going.
